speaker: Derek Lowe
title: Derek Lowe, PhD: A Medicinal Chemist’s Thoughts on Drug Discovery and the Future of Pharma
question: In pharmaceuticals, why are biologic drugs much harder to genericize than traditional small-molecule drugs?
guest: Biologics are simply a lot more complicated to manufacture and to assay than small molecules are. There are also a lot more variations you can run on them. When people talk about insulin, they are often talking about the original Banting and Best insulin, which is not what most people take—insulin has been modified with amino acid changes and polyethylene glycol chains to extend its half-life, so those neo-insulins are superior, patented new inventions. The core problem is that when you make a large protein like an antibody, there are so many variables in manufacturing because you're making them in living cellular systems or cell-derived systems with enzymes. These proteins undergo modifications like glycosylation and phosphorylation, and different expression systems produce different variations that can perform differently in the body. That makes it tricky to assay these drugs and prove your substance is identical to the biologic on the market. For a small molecule, analytical techniques like NMR and mass spec are very solid; for large biologics, it's much more difficult. Even with FDA biogeneric frameworks emerging, companies realized a good biologic effectively meant a huge patent extension.

points.core: Biologics are manufactured inside living cellular systems that introduce complex process variability.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Biologics are harder to copy because they are fundamentally different kinds of products. A small-molecule drug like aspirin is a simple, well-defined chemical made by predictable synthesis, so a generic maker can produce an identical molecule and prove it with straightforward lab tests and a small bioequivalence study.

Biologics, such as monoclonal antibodies, are large, complex proteins, often hundreds to a thousand times bigger, produced by living cells. Their final structure, including folding and sugar attachments (glycosylation), depends on the specific cell line and on manufacturing conditions, which are proprietary. Even the originator sees batch-to-batch variation, so a competitor using a different cell line can only make something "highly similar," never identical. Small differences can affect efficacy or trigger immune reactions.

As a result, regulators require "biosimilars" to go through a heavier approval pathway: extensive analytical characterization, and usually clinical studies of pharmacokinetics, immunogenicity and sometimes efficacy. Development typically costs $100–300 million and takes many years, versus a few million for a generic. Dense patent thickets, longer exclusivity periods (12 years in the US), and limits on automatic pharmacy substitution add further barriers.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Traditional small-molecule drugs, like aspirin, have simple, fixed chemical formulas made of a few dozen atoms. Manufacturers can synthesize identical molecular copies through predictable chemical reactions and win approval simply by proving chemical equivalence and matching absorption in the bloodstream. Biologics, such as monoclonal antibodies, are massive, intricate proteins containing thousands of atoms folded into delicate three-dimensional structures with complex sugar attachments. Rather than being chemically synthesized, biologics are grown inside living cells using proprietary cell lines and sensitive fermentation processes. Because living organisms are inherently variable and originators guard their exact manufacturing methods as trade secrets, competitors cannot produce an identical copy—only a close approximation called a biosimilar. Even tiny differences in cell culture conditions can alter protein folding or sugar patterns, potentially reducing efficacy or triggering dangerous immune reactions in patients. Consequently, biosimilar developers face far higher technical and regulatory hurdles, requiring bespoke cell-line engineering, exhaustive analytical testing, and costly clinical studies to prove matching safety, purity, and potency.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Biologic drugs are hard to copy because of what they are and how they're made. A small-molecule drug like aspirin has a few dozen atoms and a fixed structure. Chemists can make an identical copy, and a generic maker only has to show that it is chemically the same and behaves the same in the body (bioequivalence).

Biologics are large proteins or other complex molecules, often thousands of times bigger. They are produced by living cells. Their final form, including how the protein folds and which sugar chains attach to it, depends on the cell line, growth conditions, purification and many other process details. Those details are largely trade secrets, and as the industry saying goes, "the process is the product." A competitor can't reproduce the exact molecule. It can only make a "biosimilar" that is highly similar, with no meaningful clinical differences.

Proving that is expensive. It takes extensive analytical work, often clinical trials, and immunogenicity testing, which can cost $100–300 million over many years, compared with a few million for a generic. Biologics also get longer data exclusivity (12 years in the US), and originators build dense patent thickets around them. Biosimilars are not automatically substituted at the pharmacy the way generics are, either. Together, these factors mean fewer competitors enter and prices fall less.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Traditional small-molecule drugs are relatively simple chemical compounds synthesized through predictable, reproducible reactions. Because their exact molecular structure can be fully characterized and replicated, generic manufacturers only need to prove chemical identity and bioequivalence in a small number of volunteers to win regulatory approval.

Biologic drugs, by contrast, are enormous, structurally complex proteins produced inside living systems such as bacteria, yeast, or mammalian cells. Their therapeutic effect and safety depend not just on their amino acid sequence, but also on intricate three-dimensional folding and delicate chemical attachments like sugar chains. Because even tiny changes in cell lines, nutrients, or purification conditions alter the final product, it is virtually impossible to create an exact copy, only a closely matching "biosimilar."

Consequently, regulators cannot rely on simple bioequivalence tests. Biosimilar developers must invest heavily in reverse-engineering proprietary manufacturing processes, building specialized facilities, and running costly clinical trials to prove comparable efficacy, safety, and immunogenicity. These scientific, manufacturing, and regulatory hurdles make developing biosimilars far slower and more expensive than traditional generics.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Small-molecule drugs usually have a well-defined chemical structure that another manufacturer can reproduce. A generic manufacturer generally needs to show that its product contains the same active ingredient and delivers it into the bloodstream at a comparable rate and extent.

Most biologics, such as therapeutic antibodies, are large, complex proteins made in living cells. Even with the same amino acid sequence, differences in the cell line, growth conditions, or purification process can affect protein folding, attached sugars, or the tendency of proteins to clump. These differences can affect how the drug works or how the immune system responds to it. Some variability exists even between batches of the original product.

Regulators therefore approve follow-on biologics as *biosimilars*. Manufacturers must show that their product is highly similar to the original and has no clinically meaningful differences in safety, purity, or potency. That requires extensive laboratory comparisons and, where needed, studies in people. Developing a manufacturing process that consistently produces a highly similar product adds further cost and complexity.
